summary: United Rentals is trading at a below-market forward multiple. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple.
body: I'm a firm believer in investing in what you know—and what you use. During a recent visit to my parents' New Hampshire property, my brother and I tackled overdue maintenance, and having the right equipment on hand was critical to finish the work in the limited time we had. He and I rented both a compact track loader (CTL, not pictured) and a bulldozer (pictured above) from United Rentals (NYSE: URI) to push through some of the heavier work. For those who may not be familiar with the company, United Rentals can quickly deploy heavy equipment to a remote site. Here's why I believe it sets up well for a defined-risk, moderately bullish options trade. The good news is that United Rentals is currently trading at a below-market forward multiple — both on a Price-to-Earnings (P/E) basis, currently ~17.3x forward estimates of ~$61.10/share, and on an Enterprise Value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) basis at ~8.8x $9.25 billion in FYE2027 EBITDA. This despite the fact that the company is compounding revenues, earnings, and EBITDA at a noticeably faster clip than the cap-weighted S&P 500. Effectively, one can buy superior, market-beating growth at a discounted market multiple. The recent third-quarter earnings confirmed this trajectory. URI delivered a beat and raise, pointing to robust underlying demand across its end markets, and the sell-side is scrambling to catch up, revising its forward estimates upward. Improving earnings estimates is one of the most reliable, time-tested short-term investment factors. Stocks with positive estimate revisions tend to meaningfully outperform those burdened with declining estimates in the short term. The macro backdrop provides a sturdy foundation for this growth. We are in the midst of a broader nonresidential construction recovery, which has driven an environment of improving and resilient rental rates. Although admittedly a potential slowdown in data center construction could become a future headwind, broader infrastructure demand remains robust. A balanced view requires acknowledging the risks. While URI looks cheap relative to the broader market, it is not exactly cheap relative to its own history. The stock is currently trading roughly 20% to 25% above its five-year average multiple. One could easily argue that the historical multiple was simply too cheap for a business of this quality, scale, and capital efficiency. Still, mean reversion back to historical levels of "cheapness" remains a downside risk. This brings us to the options market. When you have a stock with solid momentum, fundamentals, and positive estimate revisions, but you're hesitant to pay a premium to its historical valuation, outright unhedged equity accumulation isn't always the optimal route. Instead, selling cash-covered puts offers a highly strategic entry mechanism. With URI's implied volatility currently hovering in the 42% to 45% range, the options market is pricing in enough movement to offer a decent premium. By selling a cash-covered put, we acknowledge both the good and the bad. It respects the aggressive growth, market share capture, and the recent beat-and-raise quarter, while appropriately hedging against the risk of that elevated historical multiple. If the stock continues its upward march, the puts expire worthless, and we pocket a high-probability yield that easily beats fixed income. If the stock pulls back—perhaps toward that 5-year average multiple—we are assigned the shares at a lower effective cost basis, which, if it happens, we could lower even further by writing upside covered calls against it. (This approach to entering a stock, then writing covered calls if assigned, is sometimes referred to as "the wheel strategy"). That leaves the Australian dollar with little support from rate expectations, at a time when it is already exposed to swings in AI-linked equities. Front-end Australian bond yields are the most sensitive to any shift toward pricing an earlier end to the tightening cycle. Above-target inflation and petrol prices near A$2.40 a litre keep the RBA from pivoting quickly. Lower oil prices would be the fastest route to relief for households. Australian households are feeling as gloomy as they have only in genuine crises, and the RBA’s own rate hikes are a big part of why. Australian consumer sentiment fell to a four-year low in November, as rising living costs and another interest rate hike pushed households deeper into pessimism, a Westpac and Melbourne Institute survey showed on Tuesday. The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index dropped 2.7% to 78.2 from 80.4 in October, its weakest reading since late 2022. Westpac noted that, apart from that period, readings this low have only been seen in the economy’s darkest moments, including the onset of the COVID pandemic, the global financial crisis and the recessions of the early 1990s and 1980s. Cost-of-living pressure remains the main driver. Over the past month petrol prices have pushed toward A$2.40 a litre and official inflation has reached 4.3%. The Reserve Bank of Australia has also raised the cash rate by another 25 basis points to 4.85%, an 18-year high. Westpac said any lift from the US midterm results had been swamped by inflation and rate worries. Sentiment among mortgage holders slumped to a record low on data back to 1994. The November fall was led by a sharp deterioration in near-term expectations for the economy, which dropped to their weakest since August 2020. Households also turned negative on house prices for the first time since late 2022, and more than 70% of consumers expect mortgage rates to rise further over the coming year. Job-loss fears are edging higher, though Westpac described consumers as on edge rather than alarmed. For the RBA, the survey adds to evidence that its five hikes this year are biting hard on rate-sensitive parts of the economy. Westpac expects the central bank to pause at its December 7-8 meeting to assess the impact of its tightening. It does not expect a hike in February either, though it cautioned that high inflation will continue to test the bank’s resolve. The weak mood is a concern for retailers heading into Christmas. Even so, Westpac said gift-spending intentions have held up better than headline sentiment suggests, with mortgage holders the most likely to cut back. Britons spent more in October, but mostly on fuel and food, and they feel gloomier about the economy than at any point since April. UK retail sales grew modestly in October, the British Retail Consortium said on Tuesday. Higher petrol prices, caution ahead of the Budget and shoppers holding off for Black Friday deals kept a lid on spending, even as a separate card-spending survey from Barclays showed the strongest growth in more than a year. Total retail sales rose 1.5% from a year earlier, up from 1.3% in September and the strongest increase since June, according to the BRC. Like-for-like sales, which strip out changes in store space, rose 1.1% after 1.0% the previous month. Food sales climbed 3.2% while non-food sales were flat, a split that points to price-driven grocery spending rather than a broad pickup in discretionary demand. The BRC noted that sales of cupboard staples rose modestly after the government advised households to stock up for emergencies. Commentary accompanying the survey described overall growth as modest, citing higher household costs, caution ahead of the Budget and consumers waiting for Black Friday discounts. Barclays’ data, which covers card spending on a wider range of goods and services, painted a firmer picture. Consumer spending rose 2.3% year on year in October, up from 2.0% in September and the biggest increase since July 2025. Essential spending grew 3.1%, driven by a 22.7% jump in spending on fuel, while non-essential spending rose 1.9%. Entertainment had its strongest month since September 2024 as tickets for the Glastonbury music festival went on sale. The fuel figure shows how higher energy costs are inflating headline spending. Much of the increase reflects households paying more at the pump rather than buying more, which squeezes budgets for other goods. That strain shows up in sentiment. Barclays said consumer confidence in the UK economy was at its weakest since April, suggesting households remain wary despite the steadier spending figures. Non-food sales were flat, and Black Friday is likely to pull some purchases into late November. Australian business conditions fell to their weakest level in six years in October as forward orders dropped sharply, a National Australia Bank survey showed on Tuesday. The survey’s business conditions index slipped 1 point to -2, the lowest reading since August 2020. Business confidence also fell 1 point, to -15, far below its long-run average of +5. That could temper the yen’s gains from rate expectations in the near term. A strong hawkish tone in the Summary would likely outweigh one weak, volatile data point, leaving December pricing broadly intact. If the Summary instead shows members giving more weight to soft demand, the data would reinforce a slower path and leave the yen more exposed. Japanese households are still keeping their wallets shut despite higher pay, giving the BoJ’s cautious members fresh ammunition just as the hawks push for December. Japanese household spending fell far more sharply than expected in September. The weak consumption signal comes just as the Bank of Japan publishes the Summary of Opinions from its October meeting and markets weigh the case for a December rate hike. Spending fell 6.8% from a year earlier, internal affairs ministry data showed, against a median forecast for a 3.1% decline. On a seasonally adjusted monthly basis, spending dropped 2.8%, compared with expectations for a 0.3% rise. It was the tenth consecutive year-on-year decline and far deeper than July’s 3.6% drop, which had itself been the steepest in 30 months. August had shown a smaller 3.1% fall. The weakness persists even though real wages had risen for eight straight months through August, suggesting higher pay is still being absorbed by elevated living costs rather than spent. The household survey is volatile and based on a relatively small sample, so economists tend to treat single readings with caution. Even so, the run of declines is now hard to dismiss. The data feed directly into the debate inside the BoJ. The central bank held its policy rate at 1.25% on October 30 in an 8-1 vote, with board member Hajime Takata dissenting in favour of a hike to 1.5%. It said underlying inflation is now generally consistent with its 2% target and judged price risks to be skewed to the upside, while trimming its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to 0.7%. Governor Kazuo Ueda later softened the inflation message at his press conference. The Summary of Opinions is an anonymous digest of board members’ views, released ahead of the full minutes. It will show how many policymakers see the conditions for the next hike as in place, and how much weight the more cautious members give to the economy. Soft consumption is the kind of evidence those members could cite, alongside the slightly weaker growth outlook. For now, markets widely expect the BoJ to keep its roughly quarterly pace with a hike in December, after moves in June and September. The policy board’s focus remains on inflation and wages rather than any single spending print. But a sustained slide in household demand would make it harder for the bank to argue that higher wages are feeding through to a self-sustaining recovery. It could also leave the yen with less support from rate expectations. There's always something new to learn about the markets. body: With no official annual rate, the monthly core reading carries most of the weight. A 0.3% core print would revive hawkish Fed pricing for December, likely lifting Treasury yields and the dollar and adding pressure to tech stocks still fragile after last week’s selloff. A 0.2% or softer core reading would support the case for a pause and help extend Monday’s equity rebound. Estimated annual headline figures near 4% may still dominate early headlines, so there is a risk of a knee-jerk move that fades once traders focus on the monthly detail. Lower gasoline prices during October offer some relief on the energy side. The monthly numbers should show prices rising more slowly than in September, but the shutdown gap means the annual inflation rate everyone quotes will be an estimate this time. US consumer prices are expected to have risen at a slower monthly pace in October after a gasoline-driven jump in September. But Tuesday’s report will arrive with a notable gap: there will be no official annual inflation rate for either the headline or the core index. The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October CPI at 13:30 GMT (08:30 US Eastern time). Economists expect headline CPI to have risen about 0.3% on the month and core CPI, which strips out food and energy, about 0.2%, after gains of 0.6% and 0.3% in September. A smaller boost from gasoline, which fell during October, accounts for most of the expected slowdown in the headline figure. A real-time nowcast from the Cleveland Fed points to readings of about 0.2% for both measures. The missing piece is a legacy of last year’s 43-day government shutdown, which ran from October 1 to November 12, 2025. The BLS was unable to collect price data that month and never published an October 2025 CPI report. Without a year-ago index, the agency has said it will not publish 12-month changes for October 2026 where the October 2025 data are unavailable, which covers both the all-items and the core series. That leaves economists to impute last October’s levels and estimate annual inflation themselves. FactSet’s median estimates point to headline inflation of about 4% year on year, up from 3.7% in September, and core inflation of about 2.8%, up from 2.6%. Those figures rest on a small number of forecasts and on imputation choices that vary between firms. Any annual rate quoted after the release will be an estimate rather than an official reading. Analysts see the risks to core as tilted higher. Elevated shipping costs and reinstated tariffs could lift core goods prices, while airfares, lodging and recreation services may add pressure. A pullback in owners’ equivalent rent after unusual strength in September could offset some of that. Several forecasters note that monthly core readings below 0.15% have been rare since 2022. The release is the final CPI report before the Federal Reserve’s December meeting. The Fed held rates in October, and an in-line reading would leave inflation well above the 2% target without ruling out further tightening. With no official annual figures, the monthly core number is likely to drive the market reaction. There's always something new to learn about the markets. The push reflects sweeping cost reductions, an overhaul of operating accountability after years of missed production targets and about $10 billion in capital project overruns over 18 years, as well as stronger copper prices. Vale’s third-quarter results show its average realized copper price rose 56% year over year to $15,314 per tonne, outpacing a 44% increase in the benchmark London Metal Exchange price. Usmar is now betting that redesigned projects and brownfield expansions near existing infrastructure can deliver growth at substantially lower costs and higher returns. “We aren’t just a turnaround story; we’re also a growth story,” Usmar said Monday at the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum’s (CIM) Capital Projects Symposium in Toronto. VBM has generated more than $1 billion in free cash flow this year, he added. VBM produced 382,300 tonnes of copper and 177,200 tonnes of nickel in 2025, increases of 10% and 11%, respectively, from the previous year. VBM aims to produce about 700,000 tonnes of copper annually by 2035, an 83% increase from 2025 levels. Usmar said the company has the potential to go considerably further. title: Copper price bounces after worst week since March amid scramble for metal in China
summary: The Yangshan premium for copper shipped into China climbed to a record $230 a tonne on Monday, spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled in two weeks, and deliverable stocks on the SHFE would cover less than a day of Chinese consumption.
body: Copper prices rebounded on Monday, recovering part of last week’s steep losses as risk appetite steadied, the dollar slipped and tight physical supply in China came back into focus. Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, was trading at $6.3550 a pound ($14,010 a tonne) late morning in New York, up 1.9% on the day and roughly 13% higher so far in 2026. On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper rose 0.9% to $13,890 a tonne by mid-afternoon in London, having lost 2.7% last week in its steepest weekly decline since March. In Shanghai the most-traded contract gained 0.5% to 107,430 yuan ($16,096) a tonne. “Copper is recovering as risk sentiment stabilises and tight physical supply in China returns to focus,” ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey told Reuters, adding that the rise in spot premiums shows metal remains difficult to secure. The Yangshan copper premium, which reflects demand for metal imported into the top consumer, rose to a record $230 a tonne on Monday. Copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange-monitored warehouses fell more than 24% last week to 33,848 tonnes, the lowest in almost three years, according to John Gross of The Copper Journal . That would cover China’s copper consumption for less than a day. Bloomberg reports the Singapore-based trader Trafigura, one of the biggest in the copper market, has over the past two weeks approached several producers and traders in Asia seeking to buy large volumes over November and December, and has been willing to outbid rivals to secure cargoes. Spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled over the past two weeks to a record 2,615 yuan ($392) a tonne, according to Shanghai Metals Market, while premiums for imported copper tracked by Fastmarkets have jumped more than 40% to $195–210 a tonne, the highest in data going back to 2017. On the SHFE, the spread between December and January contracts blew out to more than 1,200 yuan a tonne late on Friday, the widest backwardation since 2005. Chinese smelters are struggling to source concentrate and scrap, and a crackdown on illegal mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo – China’s biggest source of refined copper – in which the government seized more than 500 trucks and several thousand tonnes of copper and cobalt, threatens to crimp supplies further. “One of the main drivers for the tightness is the slowdown in refined production growth, which reflects the fact that smelters have been struggling for feedstock,” Morgan Stanley metals strategist Amy Gower told Bloomberg. “The demand indicators are fairly lackluster, so it does point to supply issues being the cause of the tightness in the Chinese market.” Comex depots hold 732,943 tonnes, more than double a year ago, after two years in which miners and traders prioritised shipments to the US ahead of threatened import tariffs. On paper, the surge in Shanghai premiums and spreads is now large enough to cover the cost of shipping copper from the US back to China. The hindrance, people familiar with the trade told Bloomberg, is that those cargoes would be worth far more in the US if tariffs are eventually imposed. “This is starting to become more of a question, but for it to happen I think you’d need tariffs to be definitively ruled out,” Gower said. “Our base case is that the US material will be quite sticky and will only get drawn down through under-importing.” Monday’s bounce may not hold. “Today’s move does not necessarily mark the end of the correction,” ING’s Manthey said. “Prices remain vulnerable to further weakness if broader market sentiment deteriorates again.” A Democratic sweep in last week’s US midterm elections has reduced the prospects for the Trump administration’s planned tariffs on refined copper and raised the odds of tighter restrictions on data centres, threatening both the AI-related demand and the tariff-driven stockpiling that have supported prices this year. At a time when the central bank is increasingly confident about the state of the labor market, concerns over the cost of living are what are top of mind for the Fed. "We've been moving up to what historically we'd consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. title: How AI and inflation are fueling fears of Fed hikes ahead - Mortgage Professional America
body: Expectations of a Fed increase in December are strengthening, while AI investment is worsening the inflation outlook – potentially spelling bad news for mortgage rates With just a month until the Federal Reserve’s final interest rate decision of 2026, last week’s October jobs report may have copper-fastened a December rate hike by the central bank. Mortgage rates don’t rise and fall in line with Fed rate decisions, but bond markets often price in expectations of increases – meaning the Fed’s next moves could have big consequences on the rate outlook. A Bureau of Labor Statistics report showed the labor market blew past expectations last month, adding 165,000 jobs as the unemployment rate ticked lower. Those figures reflected an economy that’s still showing decent momentum despite global trade tensions and other geopolitical turbulence. But of most interest to the US central bank could be the fact that overall inflation is still outstripping hourly wage growth, rising by 3.7% at last reading compared with a 3.1% increase in wages. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy categories, rose by 3.1% year over year in September. Investment is also continuing to flood into artificial intelligence (AI), although last week’s midterm election result sparked speculation that a new Democrat-led Congress could curb the AI boom by introducing new guardrails and increased oversight of tech companies. For now, though, a combination of factors – the impact of the US’s tariff regime, higher oil prices from the war in Iran, and AI investment – are likely to continue putting upward pressure on headline inflation, according to Oxford Economics’ chief US economist Michael Pearce. “The two big [factors] are the pass-through of high energy prices, particularly diesel and gasoline prices, to a range of other consumer goods and services – in particular food prices – and the impact of the AI buildout, which is pushing up electronics prices, has put upward pressure on software prices as well,” Pearce said last week. “We think those three shocks – the tariffs , AI buildout, and the knock-on impacts of energy prices – are adding as much as 0.8, 0.9 percentage points to core PCE inflation. If we’re thinking about core PCE inflation being 3.1%, almost all of that overshoot relative to the 2% target [is] driven by these supply shocks.” Oxford Economics is forecasting national economic growth of 2.5% next year, Pearce said, with that likely to be spurred in large part by AI. “Our estimate is that something close to one-third of recent US GDP growth has been directly or indirectly driven by AI,” he said. “That’s both just the physical capital investment in the technology, but also the rise in equity wealth, which we think is an important factor behind consumer spending as well.” Oxford Economics and the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) both see a December Fed hike ahead , while prospects of a rate increase next month swelled to 84.5% on CME’s FedWatch , a gauge of market expectations for the central bank’s next moves. title: What economic surprises can tell us about inflation - CommBank
body: CBA’s Macro Surprise Index provides a market-calibrated measure of whether Australian economic data is running ahead of or below expectations. CBA’s Macro Surprise Index tracks whether Australian economic data is trending above or below expectations, giving more weight to surprises that matter most for interest rate markets. Its latest update shows stronger-than-expected inflation is being offset by weakness in the jobs market. CBA research suggests a sustained run of upward surprises on the index can flag a greater risk of inflation exceeding the RBA’s forecasts and those forecasts being revised higher. Inflation is proving stubborn, but the jobs market is showing signs of weakness. For Australians following the interest rate outlook, the economy is sending mixed messages. CBA’s Macro Surprise Index (CBAMSI Index) offers a way to bring those signals together. Rather than looking at economic figures in isolation, it measures how they compare with expectations. Commonwealth Bank Director Fixed Income and Interest Rate Strategy Dr Hamid Yahyaei says those surprises can also provide clues about when the Reserve Bank of Australia’s inflation forecasts may need a rethink. The idea behind the Macro Surprise index is straightforward: what matters is not just what the latest economic data shows, but whether it what it reports caught economists off guard. The index tracks the gap between actual results and economists’ collective forecasts. It also gives more weight to surprises that have a greater influence on Australian interest rate markets, helping distinguish the developments that matter most. It’s therefore a measure of the unexpected, rather than just a scorecard showing whether the economy is doing well or badly. Higher-than-expected inflation, for example, can push the index upwards even though rising prices are not welcome news. A research note published by Commonwealth Bank economists following the RBA November meeting showed the Index to be sitting just below zero. Stronger-than-expected inflation was being offset by weaker labour market signals , leaving upward and downward surprises broadly balanced. “Inflation is still too high and above target, but there are signs that the Australian economy is slowing”, Yahyaei said. A reading near zero therefore does not mean inflation is no longer a concern, but it implies competing surprises are largely cancelling each other out. The research also examined whether the index could help identify when inflation forecasts were more likely to miss the mark. The analysis looked at the index’s average level over the three months before each RBA forecast. Yahyaei said large upward surprises were associated with inflation readings coming in further above the Bank’s forecasts around a year ahead, with downside surprises associated with inflation readings below the RBA’s forecasts over the same period. Higher index readings were also linked to a greater likelihood of upward revisions to inflation forecasts. The relationship was particularly visible during the pandemic, when sudden changes in the economy produced unusually large surprises and forecast misses. Those errors have since become smaller, although inflation has continued to exceed the RBA’s forecasts more regularly than before the pandemic. “Forecasting is a tough game for both the RBA and market economists”, Yahyaei said. For people watching the interest rate outlook, the takeaway is to look beyond a single forecast. A sustained run of upward surprises could signal a risk that inflation proves more persistent than expected. The index offers a way to assess that risk, but not a guaranteed guide to the next rate decision. For the latest news and announcements from Commonwealth Bank. body: The most accurate dollar-yen forecaster in Bloomberg's latest rankings is betting the Japanese currency will climb to about 147 per dollar next year, a call built on the view that the Bank of Japan will tighten far more aggressively than most investors currently anticipate. Neil Parker, head of economics and market strategy at foreign-exchange and payments firm TTT Moneycorp Limited, expects the yen to reach roughly 155 by the end of this year before extending its advance. That places him at the bullish extreme of a market that has rarely been as split on the currency's direction: the top forecaster in the prior quarter's rankings sees the yen sliding to as weak as 170 next year. The divergence rests on the interest-rate outlook. Parker projects the BOJ will lift its benchmark rate from 1.25% to at least 2%, and possibly 2.25%, a path more aggressive than much of the market has priced. On the US side, he sees the Federal Reserve delivering one more increase in December before pausing in a range of roughly 4.00% to 4.25%. "Japan may prove to be an outlier in terms of the Bank of Japan actually delivering on its promise to bring interest rates into line with where inflation is," Parker said. Japanese market participants remain divided over whether faster inflation will push the central bank to move more quickly. Consumer prices excluding fresh food and energy, a measure the BOJ watches closely as a gauge of underlying inflation, rose 2.4% in September. Parker said an acceleration to 2.6% or above could provoke a firmer policy response and shorten the path to tighter settings, though he is not convinced the central bank will act as early as December. The pace of tightening is what underpins his currency view. A further narrowing of roughly 50 basis points in the Japan-US rate differential, about what he expects by the middle to later part of next year, may be sufficient to reset investor expectations. "Investors aren't necessarily going to become overweight in Japanese assets," he said. "They just need to be less underweight." The yen has averaged about 158 per dollar this year and slid as far as 163.99 in July before Japanese and US authorities stepped in with intervention. Violent market moves have tested his projections, but Parker is reluctant to revise his outlook unless the economic fundamentals behind it have changed. His method compares market pricing for rates and inflation with his own estimates, hunting for gaps that can be translated into currency forecasts. "One thing I do is I try and block out a lot of the noise," he said. "I'm focused on no more than a few factors around the macro, rather than all the speeches or commentaries or anything else that you will hear from both Japan and also other major economic jurisdictions." The same approach put Parker atop the euro-yen rankings, although he credits a long-held bearish view of Europe's economy and some luck for that result. "The euro-yen forecast has been more fortuitous in some respects than dollar-yen," he said, citing his negative stance on the euro amid aggressive rate cuts and weak economic resilience in Europe. "Dollar-yen I think you can follow the macro a lot more." Parker entered financial markets in 1995 and has tracked the yen and other major currencies for decades. He joined London-based TTT Moneycorp in 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile. The firm also topped the latest rankings for EUR/USD and USD/CHF forecasts. Forecasting the yen was simpler earlier in his career, when the currency hewed more closely to macroeconomic fundamentals, Parker said. Even so, he does not regard it as especially difficult today, noting that the BOJ has become more responsive to data, particularly on inflation. "The construct around currency forecasting is not where you see things going," he said. "It's where you see things going relative to where the rest of the market thinks." body: Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker. But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary. The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who is accused of spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024 . Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Jensen Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman. Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust. "I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote. Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible. "In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen." Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years. An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon , Meta , Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems. Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world , and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives. body: Stronger-than-expected exports suggest physical demand for AI hardware held up through October, offering some support to Asian tech and supply-chain stocks after last week’s selloff. The import surprise is the more notable signal. If it reflects firmer domestic demand rather than just higher commodity prices, it would be a positive for commodity exporters and the Australian dollar, which also trades as a China proxy. If higher oil prices drove much of the gain, it points to the energy shock lifting China’s import bill. A narrower surplus may slightly ease trade frictions ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, though the year-to-date surplus remains very large. China’s trade engine is running hot in both directions, with AI hardware still flying out and a surprise surge in imports eating into the surplus. China’s exports grew faster than expected in October and imports surged well beyond forecasts, sharply narrowing the monthly trade surplus as trade flows stayed exceptionally strong. Exports rose 35.2% from a year earlier in US dollar terms, ahead of the 33.5% median forecast in a Reuters poll, though slightly slower than September’s 36.3% gain. Imports jumped 41.6%, far above expectations for a 32% rise and accelerating from 31% the previous month. The stronger import bill cut the trade surplus to about $105 billion, well short of the roughly $126 billion forecast and down from about $134 billion in September. The export figures add to evidence that the global race to build AI infrastructure is still driving demand for Chinese-made hardware. Economists say shipments of components such as printed circuit boards, memory chips and optical transceivers have powered the surge in outbound trade this year. The October data suggest that momentum held up even as US AI stocks sold off on concerns over the pace of the data centre build-out. Some analysts had warned that a drop in new export orders in factory surveys could signal a softer tech cycle, but there is little sign of that in the headline numbers so far. The import surge is harder to read without a detailed breakdown. Higher prices for crude oil and other commodities would lift the value of China’s purchases, and inbound shipments of chips and other components for assembly would also add to the total. The full customs data, due later, should show how much of the rise reflects prices rather than volumes. The figures arrive at a sensitive moment for Beijing. Chinese stocks have been under heavy pressure, prompting authorities to step up support measures, and trade is expected to feature when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen later this month. China’s large and persistent trade surplus has also risked antagonising trading partners, and a narrower monthly gap may ease some of that pressure at the margin. However, attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strategically important Strait of Hormuz continued to raise concerns over the security of global oil supplies. Brent crude futures fell $5.05, or 5.2 per cent, to $93.27 a barrel by 1427 GMT, after touching an intraday low of $93.21. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures also declined $4.12, or 4.5 per cent, to $86.71 a barrel. The latest decline followed a 16 per cent fall in Brent prices last week, taking the benchmark to a two-month low of $93.22. It marked the steepest weekly decline since the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic. Trump said on Sunday that he was highly unlikely to authorise fresh attacks on Iran as long as negotiations to end the conflict made progress. His remarks eased fears of further military escalation and reduced the geopolitical risk premium that had supported crude prices. However, the situation remains uncertain, with both Washington and Tehran reporting attacks on shipping in or near the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy transportation routes. Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen said oil prices continued to decline on expectations of a possible US-Iran peace agreement rather than any concrete indication of diplomatic progress. He added that Trump's latest comments, suggesting that renewed strikes against Iran were highly unlikely, had increased downward pressure on crude prices. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said weakness in the physical oil market, supported by continued relatively high flows from the Middle East, was another factor weighing on prices. In a report on Monday, Morgan Stanley highlighted further signs of weakness in the physical market. Dated Brent, a benchmark used to price physical crude cargoes worldwide, had weakened to a discount against the nearby Brent futures contract. The development indicates that immediate demand for physical oil is softening, despite continuing geopolitical uncertainties in the Middle East. Trump had previously hinted at the possibility of resuming military attacks against Iran following last week's US midterm elections. However, there has been no indication of a large-scale American military operation. Iran, meanwhile, has warned that any renewed attacks would invite retaliation against US and Israeli targets, raising concerns about a possible escalation across the region. Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade, described Trump's latest remarks as more measured but said the oil market was still waiting to determine whether the midterm election results had brought about a lasting change in his approach to the conflict or whether the comments represented another temporary shift in tone. Apart from geopolitical developments, concerns about an emerging global oil surplus are also putting pressure on prices. Some analysts believe the market is moving towards excess supply as high crude prices weigh on consumption and weaken demand. The prospect of increased availability of oil, combined with expectations of reduced tensions between Washington and Tehran, has encouraged investors to reassess the outlook for global energy markets. JPMorgan estimated that the global oil market recorded a surplus of 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, according to a report released last week. The combination of easing fears of military escalation, relatively strong oil flows from the Middle East and weakening physical market conditions has added to the downward pressure on crude benchmarks.
